title: Stars Erase the Smallest Letter
statement:
You get a string s made of lowercase letters and '*' characters. Handle the stars from left to right. Each star deletes itself and one letter to its left that is still present. That letter must be a smallest one among the letters still present to its left.

When the smallest letter has several surviving copies to the left of the star, you choose which copy goes. Make every choice so that the final string is as small as possible in dictionary order, and return that string. It is guaranteed that every star has at least one surviving letter to its left.

examples.why: The star must delete an 'a'. Deleting the later one gives "acb"; deleting the first gives "cab", which is larger.
The first star sees c, b and deletes b. The second sees c, a and deletes a. Then d stays.
Each star deletes one 'z'. Nothing is left.

constraints: s has only lowercase letters and '*'
Every star has a surviving letter to its left
hints: Which letter a star deletes is fixed: the smallest one present. The only choice is which copy. Which copy hurts the result least?
Removing a copy shifts everything after it one place left. Removing the rightmost copy of the smallest letter keeps the early small letters at the front, where they matter most.
Keep one stack of positions per letter. A star finds the first non-empty stack from 'a' upward and pops it. At the end, rebuild the string from the positions that survived.

explain.intuition:
The star has no say about which letter goes: it must be the smallest one present, say 'a'. It only picks which copy. Compare two copies at positions i < j. Deleting j leaves position i holding 'a'; deleting i puts whatever came after it there, and that is never smaller than 'a', since nothing to the left of the star is. So deleting the rightmost copy is always at least as good.

That turns the task into bookkeeping. Keep a stack of positions for each of the 26 letters. A star scans letters from 'a' up, finds the first non-empty stack and pops its top, which is the rightmost copy. Mark that position deleted, and at the end join the letters that are still standing.
steps: Create 26 empty stacks and a deleted flag per position.
Walk the string. A letter pushes its index onto its letter's stack.
A star marks itself deleted, finds the smallest letter whose stack is non-empty, pops the top index and marks it deleted.
Join every character that is not deleted, in order, and return it.
pitfalls: Deleting the leftmost copy of the smallest letter. In "acab*" that gives "cab" instead of "acb".
Deleting the letter just before the star, like a backspace. The rule is about the smallest letter, not the nearest one.
Building the answer with repeated string slicing. Every slice copies the string, which makes the whole thing O(n²).

solutions.title: Scan left for every star
solutions.idea: For each star, walk left over surviving letters, find the smallest letter and its rightmost surviving copy, and delete it.

solutions.title: One stack of positions per letter
solutions.idea: Each letter's stack holds its surviving positions, newest on top. A star pops from the smallest non-empty stack, which is the rightmost copy of the smallest letter.

followups: Solve it with a min-heap of (letter, −index) pairs instead of 26 stacks. What does each version cost when the alphabet is huge?
What if each star had to delete the largest letter to its left and you wanted the largest final string?
lcTitle: Lexicographically Minimum String After Removing Stars
